title: What is DSA and Its Patterns?
description: Learn what Data Structures and Algorithms are and understand common problem-solving patterns

sections.title: 5. Part 2. Core Techniques

blocks.text: DSA stands for Data Structures and Algorithms. It is the study of how to store data efficiently and how to solve problems step by step using that data.

Think of it this way a data structure is how you organise your data (like a shelf, a stack, or a map), and an algorithm is the set of steps you follow to get something done with that data (like finding the shortest path or sorting a list).
Without DSA, your code works but slowly. When you have millions of users or massive data, a bad approach can take hours. A good one takes milliseconds.
Before starting DSA, make sure you are comfortable with the basics of a programming language such as Java, Python, or C++.

items: Choose a language like Java, Python, or C++. Before starting DSA, make sure you are comfortable with the basics such as arrays, loops, functions, and classes.
Begin your DSA journey with Arrays and Strings. These topics form the foundation for many other problem-solving patterns.
Avoid jumping randomly between topics. Follow a structured order such as: Arrays → HashMap → Two Pointers → Sliding Window → Stack → Binary Search → and so on.
Focus on understanding the pattern, not memorising solutions. Solve about 5 problems for each pattern to learn how the pattern applies in different situations.
DSA patterns repeat frequently. After learning 5–6 patterns, go back and re-solve earlier problems to strengthen your pattern recognition and problem-solving skills.

blocks.text: A pattern is a reusable approach that solves a family of problems. Instead of solving every problem from scratch, you recognise which pattern fits and apply it.
There are 27 core patterns in DSA. Once you know all 27, most Leetcode problems start to feel familiar because they are just variations of patterns you already know.
<u>Before starting, let’s go through all the patterns briefly so that you can become familiar with them.</u>
Build a strong base in DSA and gain the skills needed to start solving problems confidently.
A way of solving problems using arrays by leveraging indexing, traversal, and element manipulation.
Arrays store elements in a contiguous block of memory, meaning each element sits right next to the next one. Because of this, you can access any element instantly using its index (O(1)).
Iterate through the array and perform operations like searching, updating, comparing, or rearranging elements.
Since index access is O(1), the main goal is to avoid unnecessary re-scans and track useful information while traversing.
Many problems require checking every element. So we traverse once and update a variable (like max, sum, count) while scanning the array.
Think of an array like numbered lockers. You go directly to the locker using its index, no searching needed.
A way of solving problems that involve text by treating the string as a sequence of characters.
In Java, strings are immutable, meaning once a string is created it cannot be changed. Any modification actually creates a new string, which makes repeated concatenation expensive.
Traverse the string character by character and perform operations like comparing characters, counting frequencies, checking patterns, or building new strings.
If you need to build or modify a string inside a loop, use StringBuilder instead of + to avoid O(n²) time complexity.
Many problems require processing each character of a string. So we traverse once and track information like frequency, matches, or patterns.
Think of a string like a sentence printed on a strip of paper. You can read it easily, but if you want to change one letter, you must rewrite the whole strip that’s immutability.
A way of solving problems by working directly with the binary representation of numbers.
Every integer in memory is stored as a sequence of 1s and 0s.
Bit operations work very close to the hardware level, making them extremely fast (O(1)).
Use bitwise operators like AND (&), OR (|), XOR (^), NOT (~), and bit shifts (<<, >>) to check, set, clear, or toggle bits efficiently.
This property helps solve many problems involving finding unique numbers or cancelling pairs.
When numbers appear in pairs, XOR cancels them out because
Think of XOR like a light switch. Flip it once → ON. Flip it again with the same value → OFF. Pairs cancel out. Only the unpaired one survives.

content.title: 5. Part 2. Core Techniques

blocks.text: Learn the main problem-solving techniques used to solve most DSA problems efficiently.
A way of solving problems using key-value storage for very fast data lookup.
A hash function converts a key into an array index, telling you exactly where to store or find the value no scanning required.
Average lookup, insert, and update operations happen in O(1) time.
Store elements or their frequencies in a HashMap and quickly check, insert, or update values while processing data.

Golden rule:

If you see a brute-force solution with two nested loops (O(n²)), there is often a HashMap solution that reduces it to O(n).
Many problems require fast lookups like checking duplicates, counting frequencies, or tracking previously seen values. A HashMap lets us store and retrieve this information instantly.
A technique where two index variables move through a data structure usually a sorted array or string to solve problems efficiently.
Instead of checking every pair (O(n²)), we use the sorted order to make smart pointer movements, reducing the solution to O(n).
Start two pointers at different positions typically one at the start and one at the end.

If the result is too small → move the left pointer right
If the result is too large → move the right pointer left
When the array is sorted, we can use pointer movement instead of checking every pair, which removes the need for nested loops.

KEY SIGNAL

If a problem mentions a sorted array and asks about pairs, sums, or subarrays, Two Pointers is often the right approach.
A technique that precomputes cumulative sums of an array so any range sum query can be answered in O(1) time.
You pay the O(n) cost once to build the prefix array, and after that every query becomes instant.
Build a prefix array where each index stores the sum of all elements from the start up to that index.
This avoids looping through the range again.
When problems ask for multiple range sum queries, recalculating each range would take O(n) every time. Prefix sum stores cumulative totals once, making each query O(1).
Think of it like the running balance column in a bank statement. The totals are already calculated, so you don’t need to add transactions again.
A technique that processes a contiguous range of elements by maintaining a moving window across an array or string.
As the window moves, one element enters from the right and one leaves from the left, so we update the result incrementally instead of recomputing everything.

blocks.content:
• Move right pointer → expand window
  • If a condition breaks (window too big, duplicate found, sum exceeded), move left pointer → shrink window

blocks.text: Always track the best result while the window moves.
When problems involve a contiguous subarray or substring, we can reuse previous computations instead of recalculating the whole range.

blocks.content:
• Fixed Window :window size stays constantExample: maximum sum of k elements
  • Variable Window: window expands and shrinks based on a conditionExample: longest substring without repeating characters

blocks.text: A technique used to find the maximum sum subarray the contiguous sequence of elements with the largest possible total.
The brute-force approach checks every subarray (O(n²)), but Kadane’s Algorithm solves it in a single pass O(n).
Traverse the array while maintaining a running sum (currentSum).

blocks.content:
• Extend the current subarray
  • Or start a new subarray from this element

blocks.text: If currentSum becomes negative, reset it because a negative sum only reduces future totals.
When finding the maximum contiguous subarray, a negative running sum hurts future results, so we drop it and start fresh.
Think of it like a road trip tracking net miles gained or lost each day. If the loss becomes too large, the best decision is to restart the trip from today.

6. Matrix

A way of solving problems involving 2D arrays  grids made of rows and columns.
Each cell is identified by its row index and column index.
Most matrix problems involve traversing the grid, modifying values, or exploring connected cells.

blocks.content:
• Up → (r - 1, c)
  • Down → (r + 1, c)
  • Left → (r, c - 1)
  • Right → (r, c + 1)

blocks.text: Many problems represent data as grids (maps, images, boards). So we iterate using row and column indices to process each cell.
A way of solving problems using nodes connected by pointers instead of contiguous memory.
Unlike arrays, there is no index access to reach the 10th node, you must traverse from the head through 9 pointers.
However, insertion and deletion are O(1) if you already have the node reference, because you only update pointers no shifting required.
Many problems require tracking multiple pointers to manipulate the list, such as:

blocks.content:
• Reversing a list
  • Detecting cycles
  • Finding the middle node
  • Merging sorted lists

blocks.text: A very common technique is the slow and fast pointer (Floyd’s algorithm).
Linked list problems focus on pointer manipulation, since elements are connected through references instead of indexes.

A linked list is like a treasure hunt.
Each clue tells you where the next clue is, so you must follow the chain step by step.
But adding a new clue in the middle? Just update two pointers.
Learn data structures where elements are arranged in a sequence and processed one by one.
A way of solving problems using the Last-In-First-Out (LIFO) principle. The last element inserted is the first one removed like a stack of plates.

blocks.content:
• Push (add element)
  • Pop (remove element)
  • Peek (view top element)

blocks.text: Push elements onto the stack as you process data. When a condition resolves a previous element, pop from the stack.
Stacks are useful when tracking the most recent unresolved item, such as:
Some problems require handling the most recent element first, which naturally fits the LIFO behavior of a stack.
Stacks are also how computers manage function calls.
Each function call pushes a new frame, and when it finishes, that frame is popped, returning control to the previous call.
A way of solving problems using the First-In-First-Out (FIFO) principle.
The first element added is the first one removed like a queue at a coffee shop.
Elements are added at the rear and removed from the front.

blocks.content:
• Offer (add element)
  • Poll (remove element)
  • Peek (view front element)

blocks.text: Add elements to the rear and process them from the front, maintaining the order of arrival.
Queues are the backbone of Breadth-First Search (BFS) because they ensure we process all nodes at level N before level N+1, which helps find the shortest path.
Some problems require processing data in the exact order it arrives, which naturally fits the FIFO behavior of a queue.

SPECIAL VARIANT

A Deque (Double-Ended Queue) allows insertion and removal from both ends, enabling efficient solutions for problems like Sliding Window Maximum.
Learn techniques to organise data and quickly find elements in a dataset.
A way of organizing elements in a specific order usually ascending or descending.
Sorting is one of the most important concepts in computer science, because many problems become much easier once the data is sorted.
Apply sorting algorithms to arrange data so it becomes easier to search, compare, or process elements.

blocks.content:
• Merge Sort → O(n log n), stable, uses extra space
  • Quick Sort → O(n log n) average, O(n²) worst case, in-place

blocks.text: In Java, Arrays.sort() uses different optimized algorithms internally depending on the data type.
Sorting helps simplify many problems because ordered data reveals structure that makes algorithms more efficient.
Before using Two Pointers, Interval Merging, or Greedy, always ask:
“Would sorting first make this problem easier?”
A technique used to search a sorted space efficiently by repeatedly dividing it in half.

blocks.content:
• Check the middle element
  • If it matches → done
  • If the target is smaller → search left half
  • If the target is larger → search right half

blocks.text: Each step cuts the search space in half, giving O(log n) time complexity.
Binary search is not just for finding a number in a sorted array. It is a problem-solving pattern.
Whenever you can decide “answer is in the left half or right half” using a condition, binary search can be applied.
It is often used to find:

blocks.content:
• Exact elements
  • First/last occurrence
  • Boundaries
  • Minimum/maximum satisfying a condition
  • Monotonic thresholds

blocks.text: When the search space is sorted or monotonic, we can discard half the possibilities each step, making the search extremely efficient.

Imagine guessing a number between 1 and 1000.
A smart guesser asks: “Is it above or below 500?” and keeps halving the range.
Learn how problems can be solved by breaking them into smaller versions of the same problem.
A technique where a function calls itself to solve a smaller version of the same problem, until it reaches a base casethat can be solved directly.
Backtracking extends recursion by adding an undo step make a choice, explore it, and if it doesn’t work, revert the choice and try another.

blocks.content:
• Choose pick an option from available choices
  • Recurse explore all possibilities from that choice
  • Undo remove the choice and try the next one

blocks.text: This ensures we systematically explore all valid possibilities.
Some problems naturally break into smaller identical subproblems, which makes recursion the simplest way to solve them.
Backtracking is used when we must explore multiple possible choices, such as permutations, combinations, or paths.

Think of a GPS rerouting.
It tries a road, and if it reaches a dead end, it goes back to the last intersection and tries another route.
A technique that solves a problem by splitting it into smaller independent subproblems, solving each one, and then combining the results.
The key idea is independent subproblems unlike Dynamic Programming, these parts do not overlap.
Most divide and conquer solutions follow three steps:

blocks.content:
• Divide split the problem into smaller parts
  • Conquer solve each part recursively
  • Combine merge the results to form the final answer

blocks.text: A classic example is Merge Sort, where the array is split in half, each half is sorted independently, and then the two sorted halves are merged.
Some problems can be naturally divided into smaller independent pieces, making recursion efficient and clean.

blocks.content:
• Independent subproblems → Divide and Conquer
  • Overlapping subproblems → Dynamic Programming

blocks.text: Learn hierarchical data structures used to represent relationships and perform efficient searches.
A way of solving problems using a tree structure where each node has at most two children a left child and a right child.
The structure is hierarchical with a root at the top, branches in the middle, and leaf nodes at the bottom.
Most binary tree problems are solved using tree traversal.

blocks.content:
• DFS (Depth-First Search) go deep before wide using recursion
  • BFS (Breadth-First Search) traverse level by level using a queue

• Inorder → Left → Root → Right
  • Preorder → Root → Left → Right
  • Postorder → Left → Right → Root

blocks.text: Different traversal orders help solve different types of problems.
Tree problems often require visiting nodes in a specific order, which is why DFS and BFS traversals are the core techniques.
Think of a binary tree like a company org chart.
The CEO is the root, managers have direct reports, and traversal is simply choosing the order in which you visit everyone.
A way of solving problems using a Binary Search Tree (BST) where elements are kept in sorted order.

blocks.content:
• Left subtree → smaller values
  • Right subtree → larger values

blocks.text: Because of this property, search, insert, and delete can run in O(log n) in a balanced tree.
When inserting or searching, compare the value at each node:

blocks.content:
• If smaller → go left
  • If larger → go right

blocks.text: This rule keeps the tree sorted automatically.
In Java, TreeMap and TreeSet are implemented using a Red-Black Tree, which is a self-balancing BST that guarantees O(log n) operations.
Some problems require maintaining sorted data while performing frequent inserts, deletes, or lookups, which is exactly what BST-based structures handle efficiently.
A tree structure for storing strings where each node represents one character.

blocks.content:
• A path from root to a node → prefix
  • A path from root to a marked node → complete word

blocks.text: Tries allow prefix searches in O(L) time, where L is the length of the prefix, regardless of how many words are stored.
Insert and search words character by character.

blocks.content:
• Traverse the tree one character at a time
  • Create nodes if they don’t exist
  • Mark the last node as a word end

• Follow the same character path
  • If the path breaks, the prefix does not exist.

blocks.text: Problems involving prefix search, dictionary lookups, or autocomplete systems benefit from Tries because words with common prefixes share the same path.
A trie is like a phone book organised letter by letter. You follow the first letter → second → third, and related words automatically share the same beginning.

blocks.content: • A tree-based data structure that always keeps the smallest (Min Heap) or largest (Max Heap) element at the root.

• Peek min/max → O(1)
  • Insert / Remove → O(log n)

blocks.text: Insert elements into the heap, and efficiently retrieve or remove the smallest or largest element when needed.
A common pattern is Top K problems:

blocks.content:
• Maintain a heap of size K
  • While scanning elements, remove the worst element when size > K

blocks.text: This gives O(n log K) instead of O(n log n).
Some problems require frequently retrieving the smallest or largest element, which heaps handle very efficiently.
Learn advanced algorithms and data structures to solve complex and high-performance problems.
A technique used to solve problems involving ranges, where each interval has a start and end.
Common tasks include merging overlaps, detecting conflicts, or finding gaps between intervals.
The key idea: sort intervals by start time first.

blocks.content:
• Sort intervals by start time
  • Traverse from left to right
  • Check if intervals overlap

• If they overlap → merge them by extending the end tomax(b, d).
  • If they don’t overlap → add the current interval to the result.

blocks.text: Sorting intervals reveals overlaps naturally, allowing us to process them in a single linear scan.
A technique focused on designing custom data structures to meet specific time complexity requirements.
These problems test whether you can combine multiple basic structures to achieve behaviors that a single structure cannot provide alone for example O(1) insert and O(1) getMin at the same time.

blocks.content:
• Operations required
  • Target time complexity

blocks.text: Then combine structures whose strengths complement each other.

blocks.content:
• HashMap + Doubly Linked List → LRU Cache
  • Two Stacks → Queue with O(1) operations
  • HashMap + Stack → Min Stack with O(1) getMin

blocks.text: Some problems require multiple operations to be fast at the same time, which usually means combining multiple data structures.
A technique where you always choose the best immediate option at each step, without reconsidering past choices or looking ahead.
The key idea: a series of locally optimal choices leads to a globally optimal solution.

blocks.content:
• Choose the locally best option
  • Do not backtrack
  • Do not reconsider previous choices

blocks.text: Greedy works only when two conditions hold:

blocks.content:
• Greedy Choice Property → local best leads to global best
  • Optimal Substructure → optimal solution contains optimal sub-solutions

blocks.text: When these hold, greedy solutions are simple and fast.
Some problems allow us to make the best choice at each step without affecting future decisions, making greedy both efficient and elegant.
If a greedy approach keeps failing, the problem likely has overlapping subproblems, meaning it requires Dynamic Programming instead.
A way of solving problems involving connections between nodes.
Unlike trees, graphs do not have a root or hierarchy, and they can contain cycles.
Graphs model many real-world systems, such as:

blocks.content:
• Social networks
  • City maps
  • Flight routes
  • Web links
  • Package dependencies

• DFS (Depth-First Search) → go deep before backtracking
    Useful for connectivity, cycle detection, components
  • BFS (Breadth-First Search) → explore level by level
    Useful for shortest path in unweighted graphs

blocks.text: Always maintain a visited set to avoid revisiting nodes or getting stuck in cycles.
Many problems involve relationships or connections between entities, which naturally form a graph structure.
Think of a graph like a city map.

blocks.content:
• Intersections → nodes
  • Roads → edges

blocks.text:
BFS finds the route with fewest steps,
Dijkstra’s finds the shortest distance,
DFS explores one road fully before trying another.
A technique for solving problems where the same smaller subproblems appear multiple times.
Instead of recomputing them, we solve each subproblem once, store the result, and reuse it. This often converts exponential recursion into polynomial time.

blocks.content:
• Top-down (Memoization) → use recursion and cache results of subproblems
  • Bottom-up (Tabulation) → start from base cases and build the solution iteratively

blocks.text: Both solve the same problem, but bottom-up is often faster because it avoids recursion overhead.
When a recursive solution repeatedly solves the same subproblems, storing results avoids duplicate work and greatly improves efficiency.
Dynamic Programming is like filling a spreadsheet.
Start with known values, compute new cells using previous ones, and by the time you reach the final cell, the answer is already prepared.
A way of solving problems using mathematical formulas and geometric concepts.
Many DSA problems hide a simple mathematical insight that can replace a complex algorithm with a direct formula.

blocks.content:
• Prime numbers
  • GCD / LCM
  • Modular arithmetic
  • Geometric orientation

blocks.text: Use mathematical properties and formulas to compute results efficiently.

blocks.content:
• Sieve of Eratosthenes → find primes up to n in O(n log log n)
  • Euclidean Algorithm → compute GCD in O(log(min(a,b)))
  • Modular arithmetic → handle very large numbers safely

blocks.text: Some problems become much simpler when we recognize the underlying math, allowing us to replace heavy computation with a direct formula.
More advanced algorithms and data structures used for highly optimized or specialized problems where the basic patterns are not enough.

blocks.content:
• Union-Find (Disjoint Set)
  • Topological Sort
  • Dijkstra’s Algorithm

blocks.text: Use these when problems involve complex relationships or large-scale graphs.

blocks.content:
• Union-Find → efficiently manage connected components
    Uses path compression and union by rank, giving nearly O(1) operations.
  • Topological Sort → order nodes in a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) so each node appears before its dependencies.
    Common in course scheduling and build systems.
  • Dijkstra’s Algorithm → find the shortest path in weighted graphs using a min heap, running in O(E log V).

blocks.text: Some graph problems require specialized algorithms that handle dependencies, connectivity, or weighted paths efficiently.
These are like specialist tools in a craftsman’s workshop. You don’t use them every day, but when the right problem appears, nothing else works better.
Different companies test DSA at different depths. Each tier usually expects a different level of pattern mastery and problem complexity.

blocks.text: Understanding this helps you focus your preparation on the right difficulty level.
We can explore these patterns in more detail and solve problems for each pattern in future discussions.

My goal is to carefully go through this article and become familiar with the patterns it explains. This will help me build a strong foundation, so future discussions and problem-solving using these patterns become easier and more meaningful.
Mastering DSA comes from consistent practice and learning when to apply the right pattern.
Keep solving problems step by step and over time, complex problems will start feeling simple.
